extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (applicants, patentees, prosecutors, litigators), patent examiners, and competitors evaluating patent validity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and litigating patent obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103 after KSR v. Teleflex, including how to apply Graham factors, the role of the TSM test, 'obvious to try', teaching away, level of ordinary skill, and practical prosecution/litigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham framework for obviousness (§103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the prior art and the claims at issue, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art, and (4) secondary considerations (objective indicia) of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ultimate judgment of obviousness is a legal determination; courts should make explicit findings applying these factors and not rely on conclusory statements. The KSR Court reaffirmed that Graham remains the analytical starting point for §103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible, expansive approach to TSM (motivation to combine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motivation/suggestion/teaching (TSM) test may be used but must be applied flexibly and not as a rigid formula; motivation to combine need not be found only in explicit teachings of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation may be implicit in prior art, in the knowledge of those of ordinary skill, or from the nature of the problem to be solved; courts may consider inferences and creative steps a skilled artisan would employ. KSR rejects a narrow, mandatory application of the TSM test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrelated teachings, design incentives, market forces and background knowledge as reasons to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: A court should look to interrelated teachings of multiple patents; effects of demands known to the design community or marketplace; and background knowledge possessed by a person of ordinary skill in the art to determine whether there was an apparent reason to combine known elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sources can provide a reason to combine or modify prior art references even when no precise teaching specifically directs the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to try" as a basis for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When a design need or market pressure yields a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, and a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options and does so with anticipated success, the combination may be obvious under §103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR permits 'obvious to try' reasoning where solutions are identified and predictable and there is a reasonable expectation of success; however, it is not met where a skilled artisan would have only numerous, unpredictable options with no indication which parameters are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of hindsight should not create rigid rules
rubrics_metrics.description: While courts must guard against hindsight bias, they must not adopt rigid preventative rules that deny factfinders recourse to common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis should allow common-sense inferences a person of ordinary skill would make, subject to fact-specific scrutiny to prevent hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not limit the problem definition to patentee's stated problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and examiners should not look only to the problem the patentee was trying to solve; any need or problem known in the field at the time can provide a reason for combining elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overly narrow framing of the problem is error; consider the general problem confronting the inventor prior to the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad view of relevant prior art (analogous art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of ordinary skill may be led to elements of prior art not designed to solve the identical problem; familiar items may have obvious uses beyond their primary purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art includes textbooks, treatises, common knowledge, and references from other fields of endeavor when reasonably pertinent; the analogous art determination and level of skill in the art are critical in this assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow standard for "teaching away"
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference teaches away only if, upon reading it, a person of ordinary skill would be discouraged from following the path set out in the reference or led in a direction divergent from the applicant's path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere preference for one alternative does not necessarily teach away unless the reference criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed alternative; statements that a combination is 'less desirable' often do not teach away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for articulated reasoning and rational underpinning
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and examiners should provide explicit analysis with articulated reasoning and a rational underpinning to support a legal conclusion of obviousness; 'mere conclusory statements' are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should demand explicit articulated reasoning when challenging examiner rejections; examiners should cite adequate support for asserted general principles or knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success when combining references
rubrics_metrics.description: When all claim limitations are found in multiple prior art references, an articulated showing should include that one of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in making the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable expectation is a subsidiary requirement under the Graham framework; unpredictability in the art does not automatically preclude obviousness if a reasonable probability of success exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper determination of level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of the level of ordinary skill is crucial for both analogous art and whether one of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine or modify prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level of skill affects what is considered common knowledge and what combinations or inferences a skilled artisan could make; courts should analyze and state this explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable-results principle (combining familiar elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination of familiar elements according to known methods is likely to be obvious when it does no more than yield predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle, rooted in precedent (e.g., Hotchkiss, Great Atlantic, Anderson's-Black Rock, Sakraida), supports finding obviousness for mere substitutions or applications of known techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment appropriate when obviousness is apparent
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary judgment of obviousness is appropriate where the content of the prior art, the scope of the patent claim, and the level of ordinary skill in the art are not in material dispute, and the obviousness of the claim is apparent in light of these factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR affirmed that, in some cases, obviousness can be resolved as a matter of law when the record shows no material factual disputes relevant to obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments applicants should develop to rebut obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should be prepared to show, where factually supportable, that: (1) the level of skill in the art is low; (2) the prior art is non-analogous; (3) there is no viable reason to combine or modify prior art references; (4) the function of a claim element is not disclosed in the prior art; (5) the ordinarily skilled person lacked requisite knowledge to combine or modify the prior art; (6) the examiner's assertions of general principles are erroneous; (7) the prior art teaches away; (8) the claimed invention provides unpredictable, unexpected or surprising results; and (9) there are significant secondary considerations with a nexus to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated defenses summarize the types of factual showings that may rebut a prima facie case of obviousness post-KSR; applicants may need more fully articulated rebuttals and increased use of inventor and expert declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inventor and expert declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor and expert declarations can be used to demonstrate factual points relevant to nonobviousness and rebut examiner or challenger assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report recommends increasing use of declarations (commonly used in litigation) during prosecution when factually supportable, to provide the 'articulated reasoning' and factual underpinning that KSR and courts may require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider carefully framing field of invention and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may advantageously define the field of the invention narrowly and describe a long-standing problem unique to that field, or characterize the invention as discovery of a problem or counter to conventional wisdom, to support later nonobviousness arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While including background has potential pitfalls for claim scope, factually supportable framing may help establish distinctions from the broader prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate adequacy of PTO rejections before responding
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should carefully evaluate whether examiners' rejections include the required 'articulated reasoning' and may challenge the adequacy of a rejection where appropriate, but must be cautious in disputing asserted general principles if the assertion is supportable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the examiner's assertion can be supported notwithstanding a lack of citation, whether applicants know contrary information (duty under Rule 56), and whether to preserve arguments for appeal or litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to consider disclosure obligations (Rule 56) in view of market/design incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should evaluate whether information about design needs or market pressures that could motivate combinations might need to be disclosed to the PTO under Rule 56.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR's endorsement of design needs and market pressures as motivating factors raises questions about whether such information is material and thus subject to disclosure obligations; consult counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitor strategies for attacking patents post-KSR
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitors should consider arguing obviousness based on: (1) interrelated teachings of the prior art as a whole, needs or problems known in the field, design incentives or market forces, background/common knowledge and common sense; (2) it would have been obvious to try a claimed combination that was predictably successful; (3) the person of ordinary skill is creative and can fit teachings together without precise teachings; and (4) references expressing preferences do not necessarily teach away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR expands the range of obviousness arguments available to challengers; competitors should assemble holistic prior-art narratives and consider summary judgment where factual disputes are minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential effect on presumption of validity for art not considered by PTO (dicta)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court noted (dicta) that the presumption of validity may be diminished where relevant prior art was not considered by the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although non-binding dictum, challengers may use additional prior art not before the PTO to bolster obviousness arguments; courts and the Federal Circuit will determine how weighty this consideration becomes.
